q001: According to the fragments, DRY ("Don't Repeat Yourself") is not merely about not copy-pasting code — that's only a trivial part of it. It is about the duplication of *knowledge* and *intent*: expressing the same thing in two or more different places, possibly in totally different ways. The acid test given in the book is: when some single facet of the code has to change, do you find yourself making that change in multiple places and in multiple different formats (e.g., changing code and documentation, or a database schema and a structure that holds it)? If so, your code isn't DRY.
q002: Prototypes generate disposable code used to explore specific risky aspects of the final system (architecture, algorithms, UI, unproven or critical elements) — you throw the code away and recode properly using lessons learned, making them ideal for early, cheap identification of problem spots. Tracer code, by contrast, is lean but complete and forms part of the skeleton of the final system, providing immediate feedback under real conditions as you adjust your aim. Use the tracer bullet approach when prototype code might be misinterpreted as the real product, or when you can't afford to throw away the details, since it leaves you with a solid framework for future development.
q003: The authors call inheritance a "tax" because it is a form of coupling: a child class is coupled to its parent and all ancestors, and even code that merely uses the child is coupled to that entire ancestry chain. Instead, they propose three techniques that mean you should never need inheritance again: interfaces and protocols, delegation, and mixins and traits (Tip 51: "Don't Pay Inheritance Tax").
q004: According to the book, ETC is the umbrella principle: "every design principle out there is a special case of ETC" — decoupling is good because isolating concerns makes each part easier to change, DRY avoids the duplication that forces parallel edits, and orthogonality reduces interdependency so that (combined with DRY) systems become more flexible and easier to change, debug, and maintain. The book explicitly states that ETC is a value, not a rule — a guiding instinct to develop rather than a mechanical checklist item.
q005: No — the book says the opposite: "Don't leave 'broken windows' (bad designs, wrong decisions, or poor code) unrepaired. Fix each one as soon as it is discovered," and if there's no time to fix it properly, "board it up" (e.g., comment out the code, show "Not Implemented") to prevent further damage. It stresses that "one broken window is one too many" and that even amid a crisis (deadline, release) you shouldn't inflict collateral damage, since neglect accelerates software rot faster than any other factor.
q006: In Design by Contract, a routine's **preconditions** are what the caller must satisfy before calling (e.g., the input domain of `sqrt`), its **postconditions** are what the routine guarantees when it completes, and a **class invariant** is a condition the class ensures is always true from the caller's perspective—possibly violated during internal processing, but it must hold by the time the routine exits; if all preconditions are met, the routine guarantees all postconditions and invariants will be true on completion. When DBC is built into the language, neither party explicitly checks: the precondition is tested behind the scenes after the caller invokes the routine but before it's entered, so any explicit parameter checking must be done by the caller (the called routine never sees parameters that violate its precondition). Without language support, you'd need to bracket the called routine with a preamble and/or postamble that checks these assertions.
q009: No — the book explicitly rejects that view under the heading "LEAVE ASSERTIONS TURNED ON." It argues the reasoning rests on two wrong assumptions (that testing finds all the bugs, and that production is a safe environment), and compares turning assertions off in production to crossing a high wire without a net. If performance is an issue, the advice is to turn off only the specific assertions that measurably hurt, leaving the rest enabled.
q010: DRY and Orthogonality are two different but closely related principles: with DRY you minimize duplication of knowledge within a system, whereas with orthogonality you reduce interdependency among the system's components (DRY warns against duplicating knowledge, orthogonality against splitting one piece of knowledge across multiple components). They complement each other — used closely together, they produce systems that are more flexible, more understandable, and easier to debug, test, and maintain.
q011: A binary chop applies the divide-and-conquer idea of binary search to debugging: instead of examining things one at a time, you repeatedly split the suspect set in half and keep the half that still exhibits the problem. The book recommends it in three situations: when a stack trace scrolls on forever (rather than examining every frame), when the program crashes only on a particular dataset (chop the data to isolate the exact input values causing the crash), and when chasing a regression across releases (to pinpoint the specific change that introduced the bug).
q012: In the actor model, independent processes share no data and communicate via simple, one-way asynchronous messages — each actor processes one message at a time — so no explicit concurrency or synchronization code is needed (Tip 59: "Use Actors For Concurrency Without Shared State"). A blackboard, by contrast, acts like a combination of an object store and a smart publish/subscribe broker, offering heavy decoupling and suiting cases like image processing, group calendaring, or network monitoring where parallel processes post and consume facts. Both approaches remove a class of concurrency problems but are harder to reason about because the action is indirect, requiring a central repository of message formats/APIs and good tracing tooling.
q013: Programming by coincidence means relying on luck and accidental successes—code that "seems to work" without knowing why—which is dangerous because when it eventually fails you can't fix it, since you never understood why it worked in the first place. The authors list accidents of implementation (relying on undocumented error or boundary conditions, e.g., coding against a routine's unintended response that breaks when the routine is fixed) and accidents of context (relying on unguaranteed environmental factors like a GUI being present, writable directories, environment variables, network availability, or copied "cargo cult" code), plus implicit assumptions that are rarely documented and often conflict between developers.
q014: No — that's the opposite of what the book advises. It explicitly rejects the monolithic "heavy-enough-to-stun-an-ox" requirements document: clients don't really know what they want up front, never read such documents (sign-off is like "getting them to check the spelling in an essay written in Sumerian"), and the best requirements documentation is working code, with short user stories on index cards plus early feedback via prototypes and tracer bullets instead.
